# Python Sandboxing is Still Broken by Design

On Aug. 10, we sent Grafana a responsible disclosure letting them know we’d broken out of a Grafana Cloud IRM instance and achieved code execution. On Aug. 11, less than 24 hours later, they had fixed it.

The bug hunt revealed some deep issues in Python code sandboxes and highlighted the extent the Python ecosystem implicitly trusts CPython’s memory safety. The ramifications of that are large, and ownership of the problem is messy.

Figure 1: The “Edit Grouping template” provided an avenue for breakout [...] Python sandboxing is broken by design

## Recommendations

If you use expressive template engines or safe evaluators, their security guarantees should be considered best effort and scrutinized heavily. Rely on appropriate system-level controls to contain them or move to solutions that can provide stronger safety guarantees. Aggressively update your CPython interpreter, and backport memory safety fixes outside of CPython’s own release schedule.

This is the first part in a series of publications on sandbox escapes and memory safety in the Python ecosystem. RunSybil is continuing to explore how issues like this affect common software. Check back soon for more research on the topic.

results.title: Introducing Render Sandboxes | Render
results.content:
## Scale reliably from one sandbox to thousands

While sandboxes are new to Render, reliably spinning up isolated environments on demand is not. Render already does this for every build, more than one million times a day.

Drawing on that experience, we built Render Sandboxes to hold up whether you run one sandbox or thousands. Each one is typically ready for its first command in under one second; even faster when it’s restored from a snapshot. Expect startup time to improve through the beta.

## Your sandboxes run next to the rest of your app [...] By default, when a sandbox idles without a command, Render automatically snapshots and suspends it, and then wakes it back up on the next command. Importantly, you don’t pay for CPU or memory while a sandbox is suspended. (The default idle timeout of 15 minutes is configurable, and auto-suspend is optional.)

With the TypeScript and Python SDKs, you can also snapshot a sandbox yourself and restore it in a new one later:

## Keep each sandbox secure

Agents often need network access and API keys to do useful work. Render Sandboxes let you grant them both, while controlling where each sandbox can send data and the keys it can see. This helps protect against situations such as an agent falling for a prompt injection attack, or unknowingly running malicious code. [...] “

> We’ve long been fans of Render because it enables us to move fast, and Render Sandboxes have kept that promise. Sandboxes are the runtime for the agents in our software factory, and they let our customers securely run custom code on our platform. All in, setting up Sandboxes was fast and easy, which meant less time solving infrastructure challenges and more time solving customer problems.

## Built to handle long-running work

Render Sandboxes can run indefinitely, so an agent on a multi-day task like a codebase migration keeps its running app, processes, and memory the whole time.

results.title: Render just removed its AI sandbox time limit — and Vercel still has a 24-hour cap - The New Stack
results.content:
Not everything is ready yet. Credential brokering will initially be available only to selected customers, private networking for sandboxes is still in development, and Render has yet to settle how its shared storage will handle simultaneous writes to the same file.

## Sandboxes that resume mid-task

With this launch, Render sandboxes can stay active through a multi-day codebase migration or while an agent tests an entire application.

The bigger difference comes when a sandbox needs to resume work. Vercel limits uninterrupted sessions to 24 hours, and while persistent sandboxes can restart, their running processes start over. [...] A risk remains if a process crashes after a payment goes through but before the result is saved. Render recommends using idempotency keys to prevent duplicate charges or database writes. Shared Filesystems let sandboxes and workflow tasks access the same persistent files, even after the compute that created them shuts down.

Render says the feature is designed for “many agents reading the same repo or dataset, with each one writing its own output.” But handling “concurrent writes to the same file, including locking and conflict resolution, is something we’re still studying,” the company tells The New Stack. [...] Render tells The New Stack, it is “turning credential brokering on for small groups of customers first to make sure the experience meets our quality bar” before expanding in the coming weeks, while every developer in the beta gets outbound controls that can “block all traffic from a sandbox or allow only the domains you list.”

The company’s larger argument is that the sandbox matters less than everything around it. Developers choose Render over Vercel, the company contends, because an agent usually has to run inside a larger product and do heavy background work that needs an API staying up and holding its database connections, along with background workers, cron jobs, and the database itself.
